title: Wilderness
html:
Wilderness

The wilds of the Borderlands teem with dangerous animals and ravenous monsters.

DM Secret

This is for the Dungeon Master's eyes only. Unless text appears in a read-aloud box (like the one below), don't read it to the players.

Getting Started

The Wilderness Map displays all the regions characters can visit in this section of the adventure. The player version of this map doesn't reveal the contents of each wilderness region, only the general geographic features. Share that map with your players. The Caves of Chaos and the Keep on the Borderlands aren't labeled on this version of the map so the players don't confuse them with wilderness regions.

To begin, read the following boxed text aloud:

Your adventuring party enters the wilderness. Mysteries await you in this untamed land. Where do you want to go?

The Wilderness Regions table summarizes the regions in the order they appear within this section. If fully explored, each region provides about 60–90 minutes of gameplay.

Each region is roughly the same difficulty, but the Trail region functions as a tutorial with helpful sidebars. If this is your first time as the DM, encourage the players to start there. Otherwise, have them choose a region shown on the map.

Once the player characters choose a region, go to that region and review its "What You Need to Play" section.

Wilderness Regions
RegionDescription
1: TrailFriendly travelers and no-good bandits alike use this dirt road.
2: WoodsThese majestic forests shelter wily fey and occult secrets.
3: FensTerritorial lizardfolk and a spy for hire lurk in this wetland.
4: Tamarack StandGiant spiders plague this vast stand of conifers.

Exploring the Wilderness

Wilderness encounters occur across large tracts of unmapped backcountry. The text tells you when to use a map and monsters; otherwise, you can resolve encounters using words and imagination.

Region Descriptions

Each description of a wilderness region has the following sections:

  • Features. Important features about the region, such as its lighting, appear here. The text assumes the characters explore the wilderness during the day and camp or return to the keep at night.
  • Getting Started. This section provides setup instructions for the DM and introduces the region to the characters with thematic read-aloud text.
  • Encounters. This section presents encounters that might occur in the region. Each encounter's text details what challenge the characters must overcome.

Combat

Some encounters pit the characters against foes that mean them harm, such as wild animals or greedy bandits. See the D&D Beyond Basic Rules for how to run a combat encounter.

The following stat blocks are used in this section:

  • Bandit
  • Bugbear Warrior
  • Commoner
  • Cultist
  • Curate
  • Giant Spider
  • Gnoll Warrior
  • Goblin Warrior
  • Gray Ooze Glob
  • Guard
  • Hobgoblin Warrior
  • Jacko
  • Knight
  • Kuo-Toa Marauder
  • Lizardfolk Warden
  • Mimic
  • Noble
  • Ogre
  • Ogre Zombie
  • Owlbear
  • Pral
  • Red Dragon Wyrmling
  • Skeleton
  • Sprite Skirmisher
  • Steam Mephit
  • Stirge
  • Zombie

Resting

The dangers of the wilds keep travelers on their toes. The characters can take only Short Rest while exploring a wilderness region. To take a Long Rest, characters must visit the keep (see "Keep on the Borderlands"). For more on resting, see the D&D Beyond Basic Rules.

Leaving the Wilderness

The characters can leave the wilderness any time they choose, provided they aren't in combat. If they return to a region later, it's as they left it.

Character Advancement

In this adventure, the characters can gain a level by exploring different regions. After the characters complete at least one encounter in all four regions, everyone in the party gains 1 level. This advancement occurs only once. If the characters are already level 3, they don't gain a level for achieving this milestone.

Region 1: Trail

This dirt trail connects the Keep on the Borderlands to the Caves of Chaos and the lands beyond.

Map: Trail

Trail Features

The trail has the following features:

  • Lighting. The trail is illuminated with Bright Light.
  • Terrain. The 10-foot-wide trail is well kept and mostly flat. Spaces off the trail, however, are Difficult Terrain.

Features

This section presents special features about the region. Use these to enhance your descriptions or handle situations where rules like lighting or terrain are relevant.

The rules glossary in the D&D Beyond Basic Rules defines any capitalized rules such as Bright Light.

Getting Started

To begin, read the following boxed text aloud:

You travel along a well-kept trail east of the Keep on the Borderlands. Gnarled tree roots and big rocks mark the edges of the ten-foot-wide path.

Boxed Text

Text that appears in a box like the one in this section is meant to be read aloud or paraphrased when the characters first arrive at a location or under a specific circumstance, as described in the text.

Boxed text is included for the region in general and for each encounter in it. Read the region's boxed text aloud before choosing the encounter, then read the boxed text aloud for that encounter to begin it.

The characters continue down the trail. Along the way, they face one or more encounters (detailed in the following section). The length of the characters' journey is up to you.

Trail Encounters

Each time the characters use the trail, roll once on the Trail Encounters table to determine what the characters encounter. If this is your first time being the DM, run the encounters in the order presented.

Trail Encounters
1d4Encounter
1Looted Wagon
2Talkative Traveler
3Game Trail
4Bandit Ambush

Random Tables

You can use tables like this one to randomly determine parts of the adventure. In this case, roll 1d4 to randomly determine what the characters encounter on the trail. Alternatively, you can forgo rolling and simply choose an encounter from the table.

Theater of the Mind

While the "Bandit Ambush" encounter later in this region uses a map, the "Looted Wagon" encounter happens in your collective imaginations!

Looted Wagon

A wagon stands on the trail ahead. The driver and horses are nowhere to be seen.

The wagon was looted by bandits, who stole the horses and scared away the driver. Led by a local menace named Pral, these bandits frequently accost travelers along the trail (as happens in the "Bandit Ambush" encounter described later in this adventure).

A character who inspects the wagon can make one of the following ability checks to learn more about it. Consider these examples:

13 Intelligence (Investigation). The character deduces the wagon was ambushed by bandits.

13 Wisdom (Survival). The character discovers a striking bootprint left by Pral. The heel is monogrammed with the letter P.

13 Wisdom (Perception). The character finds treasure the bandits missed (see below).

Ability Checks

When the outcome of an action is uncertain, the game uses a d20 roll to determine success or failure. This is called a D20 Test. An ability check is one type of D20 Test. Here's how to run the ability check in the "Looted Wagon" encounter:

  • Describe the Scene. Read the boxed text to paint a mental picture of the scene.
  • Ask the Players, "What Do You Do?" If the players aren't sure how to respond, suggest ways they could glean more information, like looking for tracks.
  • Narrate the Results. The Difficulty Class (DC) for each listed ability check is 13. This number represents the difficulty of the task. If the total of the d20 and its modifiers equals or exceeds 13, the check succeeds. On a 12 or lower, it fails. The encounter's description tells you what happens on a successful check. In this encounter, nothing happens on a failed check, but the character can try again.
  • Example. The Cleric searches the wagon and makes a Wisdom (Perception) check. The player rolls a d20 and adds their character's Perception modifier (+5) for a total of 17. The check succeeds, and the Cleric finds the treasure.

Treasure

The wagon holds supplies intended for the keep: animal feed, bales of hay, and sacks of freshly milled flour. Stashed in one of the sacks is a purse that contains 12 GP.

Treasure

Treasure entries detail loot in an area, such as Gold Pieces (GP). Whenever a player character finds gold, give that player Gold Pieces equal to the listed value, which is tracked on their character sheet. Encourage players to split their treasure as evenly as possible.

Talkative Traveler

A young woman with a massive backpack and an eager smile hikes toward you along the trail. The traveler waves at you excitedly.

"Good day!" she says. "I'm Mallyn. Might you be adventurers? I ask because I've been out here looking for adventures of my own—to no avail. After camping out here for days, I still don't have any tales worth telling. Do you?"

Mallyn

Human Traveler

  • Statblock:. Commoner

This young wayfarer's heart is filled with wanderlust.

  • Easy Come, Easy Go. Mallyn doesn't get attached to possessions or acquaintances.
  • Inquisitive. Mallyn eagerly asks strangers lots of questions.
  • "Don't wander into the fens unless you're looking for trouble. The lizardfolk there don't like visitors." (True)
  • "My uncle Umbrusk runs the tavern in the keep. He hears all kinds of gossip in the taproom." (True)

Mallyn, a Friendly [Attitude] wanderer, is looking for tales of derring-do from brave adventurers. She stops to ask the characters to tell stories of their exploits.

A character can take a minute to tell Mallyn a story and make one of the following ability checks to impress her. Consider these examples:

13 Charisma (Deception). The character spins a grand yarn about a harrowing experience that never happened.

13 Charisma (Performance). The character vividly recounts a legendary story through song, dramatic reenactment, or interpretive dance.

If at least one character succeeds on the check, Mallyn thanks the party and gives them a pouch she found on the trail. Otherwise, she encourages them to keep adventuring until they have something more interesting to share. Regardless, Mallyn prefers to travel alone and doesn't accompany the characters on their journey if invited.

Treasure

The pouch Mallyn found contains 10 GP.

Attitudes

Every creature has a starting attitude toward the characters: Friendly [Attitude], Hostile [Attitude], or Indifferent [Attitude] (see the D&D Beyond Basic Rules). Regardless, creatures defend themselves in combat.

Game Trail

You spot a regal elk on the trail beside a dense thicket. Startled by your approach, the elk lopes into the thorny thicket. "Blast!" cries a husky voice from somewhere in the brambles.

A character can safely navigate the thicket to the source of the noise by succeeding on one of the following ability checks. Consider these examples:

12 Wisdom (Survival). The character follows the narrow game trail used by the elk.

12 Intelligence (Nature). The character knows how to avoid the brambles' thorns.

On a failed check, a character scrambles through but takes 1d4 Piercing damage from the thorns.

Hidden Glen

A hidden glen lies on the other side of the game trail. Dozens of elk graze here in peace. Hiding in the bushes is Haldryck, a Friendly [Attitude] innkeeper who likes to hunt. (Haldryck also appears in "Keep on the Borderlands".)

Haldryck asks the characters to keep his hunting spot a secret. If they agree, he gives the characters 5 GP and encourages them to spend it at his inn when next they visit the keep.

Social Interaction

Player characters meet many different people while adventuring. As DM, you assume the roles of these nonplayer characters, whom you can embody through either active or descriptive roleplaying (detailed below). Players also use one or both of these approaches to roleplay their characters.

  • Active Roleplaying. In active roleplaying, you speak with a character's voice and might echo their body language, like an actor taking on a role. You still need to describe things that can't reasonably be acted out.

An active approach to roleplaying Haldryck in the "Game Trail" encounter might involve you pretending to hide behind imaginary foliage and speaking in hushed tones.

  • Descriptive Roleplaying. In descriptive roleplaying, you draw on your mental image of the character, saying what the character does and how they do it.

In the "Bandit Ambush" encounter, a descriptive approach to roleplaying Pral, a smarmy bandit captain, might involve you describing his flashy smile or confident swagger. You might tell the players that he holds out his hand expectantly for the characters' gold.

Haldryck

Dwarf Innkeeper

  • Statblock:. Noble

Jovial and accommodating, Haldryck is a fast friend to anyone who visits his inn.

  • Epicurean. Good food and drink are the keys to Haldryck's heart.
  • Overseller. Haldryck advertises his inn's basic necessities—like clean sheets and doors with locks—as luxury amenities.
  • "The food at the tavern is the best in the Borderlands!" (Doubtful)
  • "My inn is the only place visitors to the keep can stay overnight." (False)

Bandit Ambush

A handsome man in a green-and-gold tunic and fancy boots saunters out of the bushes. "Hello," he says casually as he blocks your path. "I'm Pral. Perhaps you've heard of me. Who am I kidding? Of course you have!"

Pral draws a sword. "Your money and your equipment, please. This is a robbery."

Pral leads a local gang of bandits. Three Bandit hide in the nearby bushes. Pral and the bandits are Hostile [Attitude] to the characters.

If the characters don't relinquish their gold or talk their way out of the situation, Pral gives the signal for the bandits to spring out (see the "Fighting the Bandits" section).

Adjusting the Difficulty

To make the encounter easier, you can reduce the number of Bandit, or you can add another bandit to increase the difficulty.

Avoiding a Fight

As an Influence action, a character can try to defuse the situation and make one of the following ability checks. Consider these examples:

13 Charisma (Deception). The character lies to Pral to gain safe passage, perhaps by pretending to be a fellow bandit.

13 Charisma (Persuasion). The character convinces Pral that violence isn't necessary.

13 Charisma (Intimidation). The character pressures Pral into reconsidering the ambush.

Advantage/Disadvantage

Sometimes a D20 Test is modified by special situations called Advantage and Disadvantage, which reflect positive and negative circumstances, respectively. See the D&D Beyond Basic Rules for more on Advantage and Disadvantage.

In the "Bandit Ambush" encounter, Pral is Hostile [Attitude], so characters have Disadvantage on checks to influence him and thus avoid a fight.

  • Roll Two D20s. When a roll has either Advantage or Disadvantage, roll a second d20 when you make the roll. Use the higher of the two rolls if you have Advantage, and use the lower roll if you have Disadvantage.
  • Example. A Rogue tries to smooth things over with Pral by pretending to be a bandit. The Rogue makes a Charisma (Deception) check with Disadvantage.

The player rolls two d20s and adds their character's Deception modifier (+4) to both results to get two totals: 16 and 9. They use the lower roll, which falls short of the DC of 13, so the check fails—Pral and his bandits start combat! If this check had instead been made with Advantage, it would have succeeded.

On a successful check, Pral lets the characters pass unharmed. On a failed check, Pral signals the bandits to emerge (see the following section).

Fighting the Bandits

In the case of combat, read the following to begin:

Pral tsks in disapproval. He snaps his fingers, prompting more bandits to spring from the bushes with weapons drawn. In an instant, you're surrounded—roll Initiative!

Pral and his bandits are brigands, not murderers. A character reduced to 0 Hit Points by Pral or his cohorts has the Unconscious condition but is Stable. If all the characters are defeated by Pral's band, they wake up 1 hour later on the trail with 1 Hit Point—and 10 fewer Gold Pieces or no Gold Pieces if they have fewer than 10 GP—each, along with a mocking note penned by Pral. At your discretion, Pral might reappear to the characters the next time they explore this region to rob them again.

Map: Trail (Bandit Ambush)

Combat

Here's how a combat encounter with Pral and his bandits ought to play out:

  • Describe the Scene. Read the boxed text aloud. Then say, "Roll Initiative!" to signal the start of combat. Pral gets his own Initiative roll. Roll once separately for the bandits, who all act on the same turn.
  • Players React. In combat, the characters and the bandits act on their turns.

Use the D&D Beyond Basic Rules to run this encounter.

Treasure

Stashed in the bushes are the recent ill-gotten gains stolen by Pral's band. If the characters defeat Pral and his band, they find a sack that contains 20 GP and one magic item; roll once on the Magic Items table in appendix A (rerolling duplicates) to determine the item.

Magic Items

Some treasure entries contain magic items, objects imbued with arcane might. Whenever a player character finds a magic item, roll on the Magic Items table in appendix A (rerolling duplicates) to determine the item.

Region 2: Woods

North of the keep sprawls a vast forest, home to hardy oaks, meaty mushrooms, and stores of primal magic. Wherever one goes in the woods, mystery and adventure abound.

Map: Woods

Woods Features

The woods have the following feature:

  • Lighting. The thick forest canopy filters sunlight from above, resulting in only Dim Light.

Getting Started

To begin, read the following boxed text aloud:

Dappled sunlight trickles through the canopy of this old-growth forest. Felled trees, shrubs, and mushrooms dot the forest floor.

Woods Encounters

Each time the characters explore this region, roll once on the Woods Encounters table to determine what the characters encounter.

Woods Encounters
1d4Encounter
1Hermit's Hut
2Occult Ritual
3Sacred Spring
4Sparring Sprites

Hermit's Hut

After a couple of hours of hiking, you happen on a humble hut made from sheets of sturdy bark and blankets of moss. Sweet-smelling smoke wafts from its chimney. The hut's wooden door is shut.

A hermit named Xanthe lives here. Banished months ago from the keep, Xanthe is initially Hostile [Attitude] toward the characters, who she believes have come to harass her.

A character who tries to convince Xanthe that they bear no ill will can make a 12 Charisma (Persuasion) check. A successful check improves Xanthe's attitude to Indifferent [Attitude], and the hermit invites the party into her hut, where she shares her story and the rumors on her NPC Card. On a failed check, Xanthe slams the door in their faces.

Xanthe

Elf Hermit

  • Statblock:. Commoner

One of the Borderlands' oldest and wisest residents was banished from the keep for crimes she didn't commit.

  • Bad Reputation. Xanthe was wrongfully exiled for using occult magic.
  • Distrustful. Xanthe doesn't trust strangers.
  • "A spy named Jacko prowls the fens. Be wary if you meet him. He'll do anything for coin—even kill." (True)
  • "The temple's head priest is a demon worshiper." (Partially true; Xanthe is referring to Ivlis, the former priest)

Occult Ritual

Eventually, you come across an eerie statue in a forest clearing. Strange runes are etched into the stone idol. Four human figures in occult robes gather around the statue, chanting ominously.

Four Cultist conduct a ritual around this ancient statue. They belong to the Cult of Chaos, a faction that delights in death and disarray. They are Hostile [Attitude] toward those not garbed in their cult's attire but don't immediately notice the characters.

The cultists continue intoning until their ritual is complete or interrupted. If disturbed, they fight.

Adjusting the Difficulty

To make this encounter easier, reduce the number of Cultist. Conversely, you can make this encounter more challenging by adding one or more Zombie, which aid the cultists as undead thralls.

Fooling the Cultists

The cultists are Indifferent [Attitude] toward any character wearing a Cultist's Robe, which they might have obtained in the Caves of Chaos (see "Caves of Chaos"). If a character approaches in this disguise, the cultists solemnly motion for the character to join the ritual, but they begin combat if the character refuses.

Completing the Ritual

If the characters join the ritual—or observe it without drawing attention—the statue's runes begin to glow with an eerie red light. After 10 minutes, the sky darkens, and the statue suddenly splits in two with a loud crack. Moments later, a wicked, disembodied laugh echoes throughout the forest. The cultists then disband.

Map: Woods (Occult Ritual)

Treasure

The characters can take robes from the defeated cultists. For each robe they take, give the players a Cultist's Robe.

Sacred Spring

Deep in the heart of the forest, the foliage parts to reveal a tranquil grove where a natural spring burbles. Rays of sunlight create a silvery glow about the crystal-clear pool.

This sacred spring is infused with primal magic.

Healing Water

A character who takes an action to drink from the spring regains 5 Hit Points. Once a character regains Hit Points from the spring, they can't do so again until they finish a Long Rest.

Destroying the Chaos Bell

If the party has the Chaos Bell from the Shrine of Evil Chaos (see "Caves of Chaos"), a character can submerge the evil artifact in this sacred spring. If this is done at night while the spring is bathed in moonlight, the bell turns to glittering ash.

Sparring Sprites

Farther into the woods, four diminutive, winged warriors flit between oversized toadstools and mossy logs, firing needlelike arrows from tiny bows. One of them calls out to you.

"Well met, giant travelers! We are training for battle," he reports. "Care to spar with us?"

Four Sprite Skirmisher spar vigorously in this clearing. The sprites are Indifferent [Attitude] toward the characters but interested in testing their mettle against the party.

Sparring with the Sprites

If the characters agree to spar with the pugnacious fey, the bout proceeds as a nonlethal combat encounter. The sprites bow gracefully, then ready their weapons. Roll Initiative.

The sprites fight valiantly but with restraint. A player character reduced to 0 Hit Points by a sprite has the Unconscious condition and is Stable. The sprites expect similar treatment by the characters.

If all the sprites are defeated, they quickly rouse themselves and commend the characters on their tactical prowess. If all the characters are defeated instead, the sprites wait for the characters to wake up—1 hour later and with 1 Hit Point each—to thank them for helping the sprites train.

Treasure

In exchange for the characters' spirited participation, the sprites reward the party with one magic item; roll once on the Magic Items table in appendix A (rerolling duplicates) to determine the item.

Map: Woods (Sparring Sprites)

Region 3: Fens

This sodden wetland is home to dangerous wildlife, canny foes, and squelching mud.

Map: Fens

Fens Features

The fens have the following features:

  • Lighting. The fens are in Bright Light.
  • Reeds. Tall, slender reeds grow throughout the soggy wetland. Areas with reeds are Lightly Obscured and Difficult Terrain.
  • Standing Water. Shallow, soupy pools of murk pervade the fens. The water is Difficult Terrain.

Getting Started

To begin, read the following boxed text aloud:

Mosquitoes buzz about the stands of cattails and gnarled trees in these squashy, stagnant fens. Croaking frogs, chirping cicadas, and squawking birds create an incessant din.

Fens Encounters

Each time the characters explore this region, roll once on the Fens Encounters table to determine what the characters encounter.

Fens Encounters
1d4Encounter
1Flock of Stirges
2Lizardfolk Swamp
3Spy's Campsite
4Sword Ferns

Flock of Stirges

Your journey halts at a narrow creek bed stained with blood. Near the shore, a giant river rat lies dead in the mud. The carcass is shriveled as if drained of its bodily fluids.

Suddenly, a flock of horrid creatures erupts from the reeds. Each has barbed, leathery wings and a long, sharp proboscis. Roll initiative!

Three Stirge descend on the characters. These bloodthirsty creatures can't be reasoned with; the Hostile [Attitude] stirges fight to the death.

Map: Fens (Flock of Stirges)

Adjusting the Difficulty

To make this encounter easier, you can reduce the number of Stirge, or you can increase the difficulty by adding one or more Gnoll Warrior drawn here by the scent of blood.

Lizardfolk Swamp

Deeper into the fens, mounds of mud rise above the fetid water and reeds. You spot a glint of gold amid the mud.

The fen's territorial lizardfolk denizens use these mounds to conceal their treasure. Two Lizardfolk Warden hide among the reeds, watching over the mounds. The lizardfolk have the Invisible condition and are Hostile [Attitude] toward the characters.

After 1 minute, the lizardfolk appear and tersely command the characters to leave at once. If the characters refuse, the lizardfolk fight.

Detecting the Lizardfolk

As a Search action, a character can scan the mud mounds for signs of danger, detecting the lizardfolk with a successful 15 Wisdom (Perception) check.

Fighting the Lizardfolk

If a character approaches the mound or disturbs the treasure (see below), the lizardfolk leap out and start combat. Characters who failed to detect the lizardfolk before the ambush have Disadvantage on their Initiative rolls. The lizardfolk fight fiercely in defense of their possessions.

Treasure

Hidden in the mounds are 20 GP and one gemstone (worth 100 GP).

Map: Fens (Lizardfolk Swamp)

Spy's Campsite

The air is still in this corner of the fens. Just ahead, a curved stand of reeds conceals a secluded campsite with a still-smoldering firepit. The reeds sway and rustle in the muggy breeze.

This campsite belongs to Jacko, a notorious spy for hire. Jacko hides in the surrounding foliage. He is Indifferent [Attitude] toward the characters.

Detecting Jacko

As a Search action, a character can survey the campsite for clues to its inhabitant's whereabouts and make one of the following ability checks. Consider these examples:

15 Wisdom (Perception). The character spots the glint of Jacko's blade in the reeds.

15 Wisdom (Survival). The character spots faint tracks that lead to the spy.

On a successful check, Jacko emerges from the tall reeds and commends the party on finding his hideout. He then offers his services to the party.

Hiring Jacko

Plucky do-gooders aren't Jacko's usual clientele, but for 25 GP, he offers to join the characters in a single fight anywhere in the wilderness. If the party contains a Rogue or a character with the Criminal background, Jacko offers a 5 GP discount. The shady halfling advertises his services as "all inclusive" and "no questions asked" while performing a cutthroat gesture.

If a player character hires Jacko, whenever the characters roll Initiative in the wilderness, ask that player if they'd like Jacko to assist them in the fight. If so, Jacko joins the fray alongside the party. After the fight, Jacko returns to this location unless the characters hire him again.

Sword Ferns

As you trudge through the mud, you tumble into a ravine of razor-sharp ferns. To continue, you must navigate this treacherous gully.

A character who examines the ferns can make a 12 Intelligence (Nature) check, identifying the plants as sword ferns—bladelike ferns endemic to jungles and wetlands—on a successful check.

To forge a path through the ferns, each character must succeed on one of the following checks:

15 Strength (Athletics). The character hacks a path through the ferns with a weapon or stick.

15 Wisdom (Survival). The character finds a safe trail through the ferns used by wild animals.

On a failed check, the character takes 1d6 Slashing damage from the ferns on their way through the gully.

Region 4: Tamarack Stand

This hilly region's sparse trees have short, bristly needles. Forest fires and giant animals are more common in this stretch of the wilds.

Map: Tamarack Stand

Tamarack Stand Features

The tamarack stand has the following feature:

  • Lighting. Bright Light illuminates the region.

Getting Started

To begin, read the following boxed text aloud:

Conifers rise from this highland's soft, peaty soil. Squirrels skitter about the fallen pinecones and pine needles that blanket the ground.

Tamarack Stand Encounters

Each time the characters explore this region, roll once on the Tamarack Stand Encounters table to determine what the characters encounter.

Tamarack Stand Encounters
1d4Encounter
1Flash Fire
2Giant Spiders' Nest
3Hobgoblin Patrol
4Pine Seeds

Flash Fire

Your expedition stops at the bottom of a steep gorge—a dead end. As you reorient yourselves, smoke begins to fill the air, and a sudden forest fire spreads through the dry canyon.

The conflagration roars in the party's direction, engulfing everything in its path.

To escape the fire unscathed, each character must succeed on one of the following ability checks:

15 Strength (Athletics). The character scales the gorge to safety.

15 Dexterity (Acrobatics). The character leaps across the branches, avoiding the flames below.

15 Wisdom (Survival). The character cuts through a thicket of trees with fire-resistant sap.

On a failed check, a character takes 2d6 Fire damage on their way to safety.

Giant Spiders' Nest

You wander into a maze of thick webs camouflaged between tall trees. Two massive arachnids descend on you with fangs bared.

Two Giant Spider start combat, eager to make the characters their next meal.

Some characters begin this encounter trapped in the spiders' sticky web (see the "Giant Web" section). Roll a die for each character. On an odd number, the character starts their turn in the web.

Giant Webs

The giant spiders have woven a 20-foot Cube [Area of Effect] of thick, sticky webs between the trees to snare prey. The webs are Difficult Terrain, and the area within them is Lightly Obscured.

The first time a creature enters the webs on a turn or starts its turn there, it must succeed on a 12 Dexterity saving throw or have the Restrained condition until it breaks free or the webs are destroyed.

As an action, a creature Restrained by the webs can make a 12 Strength (Athletics) check. If it succeeds, it is no longer Restrained.

The webs are flammable and laden with dry pollen and old animal carcasses. If the webs take Fire damage, the entire 20-foot Cube of webs ignites, and each creature Restrained by the webs takes 2d4 Fire damage. The webs then burn away and are destroyed at the end of the turn.

Treasure

After the fight, the characters find one magic item suspended in the webs; roll once on the Magic Items table in appendix A (rerolling duplicates) to determine the item.

Map: Tamarack Stand (Giant Spiders' Nest)

Hobgoblin Patrol

Ahead of you, three humanoid warriors in battered armor argue in harsh tones as they march through the forest. They haven't noticed you yet.

Three Hobgoblin Warrior were recently separated from their squadron after a bitter defeat. The Hostile [Attitude] hobgoblins are ornery and assault the characters on sight.

Adjusting the Difficulty

To make this encounter easier, you can reduce the number of Hobgoblin Warrior. Conversely, add one more Hobgoblin Warrior to increase the difficulty.

Eavesdropping on the Hobgoblins

To listen in on the hobgoblins' argument, a character must come within 30 feet of the patrol and make a 15 Dexterity (Stealth) check. On a successful check, the character hears the hobgoblins debating whether they should ally with the bugbears in the Caves of Chaos or hire the ogre mercenary that dwells there (both are detailed in "Caves of Chaos"). On a failed check, the hobgoblins spot the eavesdropping character and start combat.

Treasure

Each hobgoblin carries a leather pouch that contains 4 GP.

Map: Tamarack Stand (Hobgoblin Patrol)

Pine Seeds

Two types of trees grow in this area: one with russet bark and ruby-red pinecones, and another with gray bark and green pinecones. Squirrels and voles scamper about, collecting seeds from fallen cones. After so much travel, your stomachs growl with hunger.

The pine seeds from either tree are tasty, but the seeds from the ruby-red pinecones are poisonous.

A character can try to identify the edible pine seeds and make one of the following ability checks. Consider these examples:

13 Intelligence (Nature). The character identifies both trees and which seeds are edible.

13 Wisdom (Survival). The character observes that local woodland critters eat pine seeds only from the green pinecones.

On a failed check, a character accidentally gathers the poisonous seeds.

Poisonous Pine Seeds

A creature that eats the seeds of a ruby-red pinecone must succeed on a 15 Constitution saving throw or have the Poisoned condition until it finishes a Long Rest.

Wilderness Encounters

The following tables present additional random encounters the characters might face while exploring the wilderness. The tables are divided by wilderness region.

To generate a random encounter in a region, roll on the table for that region or choose an encounter you like. Use the map for that region to run combat encounters where necessary.

Random Fens Encounters
1d8Encounter
1Three Gnoll Warrior scour the wetlands for treasure. The Hostile [Attitude] gnolls demand one piece of equipment or a magic item from the characters and start combat if their demands aren't met.
2Two Goblin Warrior scoop mud from a lizardfolk mound as a belated birthday present for their boss. The goblins are Indifferent [Attitude] toward the characters and ask them to rate the gift.
3A nearby bog burps out two Steam Mephit that smell like rotten eggs. The Indifferent [Attitude] mephits try to amuse the characters with noisy emissions of stinky steam.
4Two Kuo-Toa Marauder try to kidnap the characters and sacrifice them to an ancient swamp god.
5A Friendly [Attitude] Lizardfolk Warden offers to guide the party through the fens. If the characters accept, the warden leads them to Jacko the spy (see the "Spy's Campsite" encounter).
6Ahead, the corpse of a red-robed cultist lies face down in the mud. The corpse is a Hostile [Attitude] Zombie that jolts up and ambushes any creature that comes within 5 feet of it.
7Two Gray Ooze Glob hide beneath a rickety bridge, waiting to ambush the characters.
8A sudden downpour causes a flash flood. Each character must succeed on a 15 Strength saving throw to swim to dry land or take 2d8 Bludgeoning damage from the debris-infested torrent.
A Heron in the Fens
Random Tamarack Stand Encounters
1d8Encounter
1The characters meet Mallyn (see appendix B) on a daytime hike. She tells them that the pine seeds found throughout this region are delicious (see the "Pine Seeds" encounter).
2A Stirge feeds on an Ogre Zombie. Both creatures are Hostile [Attitude] toward the characters.
3The characters discover an abandoned wagon. One of the crates inside the wagon is a Hostile [Attitude] Mimic.
4A hiker (Commoner) with a large backpack needs first aid. As a Help action, a character can tend to the hiker and make a 15 Wisdom (Medicine) check. On a successful check, the hiker pays the character 1 GP as thanks. On a failed check, the hiker scolds the party and asks them to leave.
5A Hostile [Attitude] Ogre rummages about an abandoned campsite for morsels.
6A spooky tree marks the site of an occult graveyard. Four Skeleton erupt from the unhallowed ground and ambush the characters.
7Pral and three Bandit sing merrily in a clearing. If Pral was defeated earlier (see the "Bandit Ambush" encounter), the bandit leader is his twin brother, Dral. If the characters have one or more musical instruments, the bandits are Friendly [Attitude] and invite the characters to perform. Otherwise, the bandits are Hostile [Attitude] and attempt to rob them.
8A Red Dragon Wyrmling soars overhead in the direction of the Caves of Chaos. It ignores the characters and is too far away for any interaction.
Random Trail Encounters
1d8Encounter
1Three Hostile [Attitude] Hobgoblin Warrior accost the characters along the road.
2Cornflower (see appendix B), the keep's Friendly [Attitude] barn hand, invites the characters to a trailside picnic.
3Four Bandit disguised as soldiers block the road, demanding a 10 GP toll. If the characters refuse or see through the disguises, the bandits fight.
4An out-of-breath Guard chases a runaway Bandit. The Friendly [Attitude] guard shouts for help in capturing the Hostile [Attitude] criminal.
5A proselytizing Cultist tries to recruit the characters to the Cult of Chaos. The cultist is Indifferent [Attitude] but fights in self-defense in combat. If the characters accept, the cultist gives them each a small iron bell and performs a short initiation ceremony on the spot. Otherwise, the cultist curses them and continues on.
6A Friendly [Attitude] Knight bound for the Keep on the Borderlands challenges the characters to a lighthearted—and nonlethal—duel.
7Shannik (see appendix B) leads a cavalry charge from the keep as part of a training exercise, and the characters are caught in its path. Each character must succeed on a 15 Dexterity saving throw or take 2d8 Bludgeoning damage from the charge.
8A traveling Curate offers to heal the characters' wounds if they have any.
Random Woods Encounters
1d8Encounter
1A Goblin Warrior suspended in a massive web calls for help. If freed, the Friendly [Attitude] goblin helps the characters defeat two Hostile [Attitude] Giant Spider that arrive moments later.
2The characters come across a swath of trees rotted by a strange blight. A character who examines the trees can make a 15 Intelligence (Arcana) check; a successful check reveals the affliction stems from evil magic wrought by occult rituals.
3Four Friendly [Attitude] Commoner around a campsite invite the characters to camp with them for the evening; the characters can take a Long Rest at this campsite.
4Two Bugbear Warrior use a rusty log saw to fell a mighty oak. The Hostile [Attitude] lumberjacks fight any who disturb their work.
5A Hostile [Attitude] and ravenous Owlbear searches for prey. It fights the characters on sight.
6Oleira (see appendix B) the trader is picking mushrooms. She can point the characters to Xanthe's hut (see the "Hermit's Hut" encounter).
7A majestic stag appears in a picturesque clearing. If the characters approach the stag peacefully, it leads them to the sacred spring (see the "Sacred Spring" encounter). Otherwise, it flees.
8The characters are caught in a lightning storm. Each character must succeed on a 15 Dexterity saving throw or take 2d8 Lightning damage.

title: Getting Started
html:
Getting Started

The Wilderness Map displays all the regions characters can visit in this section of the adventure. The player version of this map doesn't reveal the contents of each wilderness region, only the general geographic features. Share that map with your players. The Caves of Chaos and the Keep on the Borderlands aren't labeled on this version of the map so the players don't confuse them with wilderness regions.

To begin, read the following boxed text aloud:

Your adventuring party enters the wilderness. Mysteries await you in this untamed land. Where do you want to go?

The Wilderness Regions table summarizes the regions in the order they appear within this section. If fully explored, each region provides about 60–90 minutes of gameplay.

Each region is roughly the same difficulty, but the Trail region functions as a tutorial with helpful sidebars. If this is your first time as the DM, encourage the players to start there. Otherwise, have them choose a region shown on the map.

Once the player characters choose a region, go to that region and review its "What You Need to Play" section.

Wilderness Regions
RegionDescription
1: TrailFriendly travelers and no-good bandits alike use this dirt road.
2: WoodsThese majestic forests shelter wily fey and occult secrets.
3: FensTerritorial lizardfolk and a spy for hire lurk in this wetland.
4: Tamarack StandGiant spiders plague this vast stand of conifers.

title: Read-Aloud Note
html: Your adventuring party enters the wilderness. Mysteries await you in this untamed land. Where do you want to go?
desc: Your adventuring party enters the wilderness. Mysteries await you in this untamed land. Where do you want to go?

title: Exploring the Wilderness
html:
Exploring the Wilderness

Wilderness encounters occur across large tracts of unmapped backcountry. The text tells you when to use a map and monsters; otherwise, you can resolve encounters using words and imagination.

Region Descriptions

Each description of a wilderness region has the following sections:

  • Features. Important features about the region, such as its lighting, appear here. The text assumes the characters explore the wilderness during the day and camp or return to the keep at night.
  • Getting Started. This section provides setup instructions for the DM and introduces the region to the characters with thematic read-aloud text.
  • Encounters. This section presents encounters that might occur in the region. Each encounter's text details what challenge the characters must overcome.

Combat

Some encounters pit the characters against foes that mean them harm, such as wild animals or greedy bandits. See the D&D Beyond Basic Rules for how to run a combat encounter.

The following stat blocks are used in this section:

  • Bandit
  • Bugbear Warrior
  • Commoner
  • Cultist
  • Curate
  • Giant Spider
  • Gnoll Warrior
  • Goblin Warrior
  • Gray Ooze Glob
  • Guard
  • Hobgoblin Warrior
  • Jacko
  • Knight
  • Kuo-Toa Marauder
  • Lizardfolk Warden
  • Mimic
  • Noble
  • Ogre
  • Ogre Zombie
  • Owlbear
  • Pral
  • Red Dragon Wyrmling
  • Skeleton
  • Sprite Skirmisher
  • Steam Mephit
  • Stirge
  • Zombie

Resting

The dangers of the wilds keep travelers on their toes. The characters can take only Short Rest while exploring a wilderness region. To take a Long Rest, characters must visit the keep (see "Keep on the Borderlands"). For more on resting, see the D&D Beyond Basic Rules.

Leaving the Wilderness

The characters can leave the wilderness any time they choose, provided they aren't in combat. If they return to a region later, it's as they left it.

Character Advancement

In this adventure, the characters can gain a level by exploring different regions. After the characters complete at least one encounter in all four regions, everyone in the party gains 1 level. This advancement occurs only once. If the characters are already level 3, they don't gain a level for achieving this milestone.

title: Region 1: Trail
html:
Region 1: Trail

This dirt trail connects the Keep on the Borderlands to the Caves of Chaos and the lands beyond.

Map: Trail

Trail Features

The trail has the following features:

  • Lighting. The trail is illuminated with Bright Light.
  • Terrain. The 10-foot-wide trail is well kept and mostly flat. Spaces off the trail, however, are Difficult Terrain.

Features

This section presents special features about the region. Use these to enhance your descriptions or handle situations where rules like lighting or terrain are relevant.

The rules glossary in the D&D Beyond Basic Rules defines any capitalized rules such as Bright Light.

Getting Started

To begin, read the following boxed text aloud:

You travel along a well-kept trail east of the Keep on the Borderlands. Gnarled tree roots and big rocks mark the edges of the ten-foot-wide path.

Boxed Text

Text that appears in a box like the one in this section is meant to be read aloud or paraphrased when the characters first arrive at a location or under a specific circumstance, as described in the text.

Boxed text is included for the region in general and for each encounter in it. Read the region's boxed text aloud before choosing the encounter, then read the boxed text aloud for that encounter to begin it.

The characters continue down the trail. Along the way, they face one or more encounters (detailed in the following section). The length of the characters' journey is up to you.

Trail Encounters

Each time the characters use the trail, roll once on the Trail Encounters table to determine what the characters encounter. If this is your first time being the DM, run the encounters in the order presented.

Trail Encounters
1d4Encounter
1Looted Wagon
2Talkative Traveler
3Game Trail
4Bandit Ambush

Random Tables

You can use tables like this one to randomly determine parts of the adventure. In this case, roll 1d4 to randomly determine what the characters encounter on the trail. Alternatively, you can forgo rolling and simply choose an encounter from the table.

Theater of the Mind

While the "Bandit Ambush" encounter later in this region uses a map, the "Looted Wagon" encounter happens in your collective imaginations!

Looted Wagon

A wagon stands on the trail ahead. The driver and horses are nowhere to be seen.

The wagon was looted by bandits, who stole the horses and scared away the driver. Led by a local menace named Pral, these bandits frequently accost travelers along the trail (as happens in the "Bandit Ambush" encounter described later in this adventure).

A character who inspects the wagon can make one of the following ability checks to learn more about it. Consider these examples:

13 Intelligence (Investigation). The character deduces the wagon was ambushed by bandits.

13 Wisdom (Survival). The character discovers a striking bootprint left by Pral. The heel is monogrammed with the letter P.

13 Wisdom (Perception). The character finds treasure the bandits missed (see below).

Ability Checks

When the outcome of an action is uncertain, the game uses a d20 roll to determine success or failure. This is called a D20 Test. An ability check is one type of D20 Test. Here's how to run the ability check in the "Looted Wagon" encounter:

  • Describe the Scene. Read the boxed text to paint a mental picture of the scene.
  • Ask the Players, "What Do You Do?" If the players aren't sure how to respond, suggest ways they could glean more information, like looking for tracks.
  • Narrate the Results. The Difficulty Class (DC) for each listed ability check is 13. This number represents the difficulty of the task. If the total of the d20 and its modifiers equals or exceeds 13, the check succeeds. On a 12 or lower, it fails. The encounter's description tells you what happens on a successful check. In this encounter, nothing happens on a failed check, but the character can try again.
  • Example. The Cleric searches the wagon and makes a Wisdom (Perception) check. The player rolls a d20 and adds their character's Perception modifier (+5) for a total of 17. The check succeeds, and the Cleric finds the treasure.

Treasure

The wagon holds supplies intended for the keep: animal feed, bales of hay, and sacks of freshly milled flour. Stashed in one of the sacks is a purse that contains 12 GP.

Treasure

Treasure entries detail loot in an area, such as Gold Pieces (GP). Whenever a player character finds gold, give that player Gold Pieces equal to the listed value, which is tracked on their character sheet. Encourage players to split their treasure as evenly as possible.

Talkative Traveler

A young woman with a massive backpack and an eager smile hikes toward you along the trail. The traveler waves at you excitedly.

"Good day!" she says. "I'm Mallyn. Might you be adventurers? I ask because I've been out here looking for adventures of my own—to no avail. After camping out here for days, I still don't have any tales worth telling. Do you?"

Mallyn

Human Traveler

  • Statblock:. Commoner

This young wayfarer's heart is filled with wanderlust.

  • Easy Come, Easy Go. Mallyn doesn't get attached to possessions or acquaintances.
  • Inquisitive. Mallyn eagerly asks strangers lots of questions.
  • "Don't wander into the fens unless you're looking for trouble. The lizardfolk there don't like visitors." (True)
  • "My uncle Umbrusk runs the tavern in the keep. He hears all kinds of gossip in the taproom." (True)

Mallyn, a Friendly [Attitude] wanderer, is looking for tales of derring-do from brave adventurers. She stops to ask the characters to tell stories of their exploits.

A character can take a minute to tell Mallyn a story and make one of the following ability checks to impress her. Consider these examples:

13 Charisma (Deception). The character spins a grand yarn about a harrowing experience that never happened.

13 Charisma (Performance). The character vividly recounts a legendary story through song, dramatic reenactment, or interpretive dance.

If at least one character succeeds on the check, Mallyn thanks the party and gives them a pouch she found on the trail. Otherwise, she encourages them to keep adventuring until they have something more interesting to share. Regardless, Mallyn prefers to travel alone and doesn't accompany the characters on their journey if invited.

Treasure

The pouch Mallyn found contains 10 GP.

Attitudes

Every creature has a starting attitude toward the characters: Friendly [Attitude], Hostile [Attitude], or Indifferent [Attitude] (see the D&D Beyond Basic Rules). Regardless, creatures defend themselves in combat.

Game Trail

You spot a regal elk on the trail beside a dense thicket. Startled by your approach, the elk lopes into the thorny thicket. "Blast!" cries a husky voice from somewhere in the brambles.

A character can safely navigate the thicket to the source of the noise by succeeding on one of the following ability checks. Consider these examples:

12 Wisdom (Survival). The character follows the narrow game trail used by the elk.

12 Intelligence (Nature). The character knows how to avoid the brambles' thorns.

On a failed check, a character scrambles through but takes 1d4 Piercing damage from the thorns.

Hidden Glen

A hidden glen lies on the other side of the game trail. Dozens of elk graze here in peace. Hiding in the bushes is Haldryck, a Friendly [Attitude] innkeeper who likes to hunt. (Haldryck also appears in "Keep on the Borderlands".)

Haldryck asks the characters to keep his hunting spot a secret. If they agree, he gives the characters 5 GP and encourages them to spend it at his inn when next they visit the keep.

Social Interaction

Player characters meet many different people while adventuring. As DM, you assume the roles of these nonplayer characters, whom you can embody through either active or descriptive roleplaying (detailed below). Players also use one or both of these approaches to roleplay their characters.

  • Active Roleplaying. In active roleplaying, you speak with a character's voice and might echo their body language, like an actor taking on a role. You still need to describe things that can't reasonably be acted out.

An active approach to roleplaying Haldryck in the "Game Trail" encounter might involve you pretending to hide behind imaginary foliage and speaking in hushed tones.

  • Descriptive Roleplaying. In descriptive roleplaying, you draw on your mental image of the character, saying what the character does and how they do it.

In the "Bandit Ambush" encounter, a descriptive approach to roleplaying Pral, a smarmy bandit captain, might involve you describing his flashy smile or confident swagger. You might tell the players that he holds out his hand expectantly for the characters' gold.

Haldryck

Dwarf Innkeeper

  • Statblock:. Noble

Jovial and accommodating, Haldryck is a fast friend to anyone who visits his inn.

  • Epicurean. Good food and drink are the keys to Haldryck's heart.
  • Overseller. Haldryck advertises his inn's basic necessities—like clean sheets and doors with locks—as luxury amenities.
  • "The food at the tavern is the best in the Borderlands!" (Doubtful)
  • "My inn is the only place visitors to the keep can stay overnight." (False)

Bandit Ambush

A handsome man in a green-and-gold tunic and fancy boots saunters out of the bushes. "Hello," he says casually as he blocks your path. "I'm Pral. Perhaps you've heard of me. Who am I kidding? Of course you have!"

Pral draws a sword. "Your money and your equipment, please. This is a robbery."

Pral leads a local gang of bandits. Three Bandit hide in the nearby bushes. Pral and the bandits are Hostile [Attitude] to the characters.

If the characters don't relinquish their gold or talk their way out of the situation, Pral gives the signal for the bandits to spring out (see the "Fighting the Bandits" section).

Adjusting the Difficulty

To make the encounter easier, you can reduce the number of Bandit, or you can add another bandit to increase the difficulty.

Avoiding a Fight

As an Influence action, a character can try to defuse the situation and make one of the following ability checks. Consider these examples:

13 Charisma (Deception). The character lies to Pral to gain safe passage, perhaps by pretending to be a fellow bandit.

13 Charisma (Persuasion). The character convinces Pral that violence isn't necessary.

13 Charisma (Intimidation). The character pressures Pral into reconsidering the ambush.

Advantage/Disadvantage

Sometimes a D20 Test is modified by special situations called Advantage and Disadvantage, which reflect positive and negative circumstances, respectively. See the D&D Beyond Basic Rules for more on Advantage and Disadvantage.

In the "Bandit Ambush" encounter, Pral is Hostile [Attitude], so characters have Disadvantage on checks to influence him and thus avoid a fight.

  • Roll Two D20s. When a roll has either Advantage or Disadvantage, roll a second d20 when you make the roll. Use the higher of the two rolls if you have Advantage, and use the lower roll if you have Disadvantage.
  • Example. A Rogue tries to smooth things over with Pral by pretending to be a bandit. The Rogue makes a Charisma (Deception) check with Disadvantage.

The player rolls two d20s and adds their character's Deception modifier (+4) to both results to get two totals: 16 and 9. They use the lower roll, which falls short of the DC of 13, so the check fails—Pral and his bandits start combat! If this check had instead been made with Advantage, it would have succeeded.

On a successful check, Pral lets the characters pass unharmed. On a failed check, Pral signals the bandits to emerge (see the following section).

Fighting the Bandits

In the case of combat, read the following to begin:

Pral tsks in disapproval. He snaps his fingers, prompting more bandits to spring from the bushes with weapons drawn. In an instant, you're surrounded—roll Initiative!

Pral and his bandits are brigands, not murderers. A character reduced to 0 Hit Points by Pral or his cohorts has the Unconscious condition but is Stable. If all the characters are defeated by Pral's band, they wake up 1 hour later on the trail with 1 Hit Point—and 10 fewer Gold Pieces or no Gold Pieces if they have fewer than 10 GP—each, along with a mocking note penned by Pral. At your discretion, Pral might reappear to the characters the next time they explore this region to rob them again.

Map: Trail (Bandit Ambush)

Combat

Here's how a combat encounter with Pral and his bandits ought to play out:

  • Describe the Scene. Read the boxed text aloud. Then say, "Roll Initiative!" to signal the start of combat. Pral gets his own Initiative roll. Roll once separately for the bandits, who all act on the same turn.
  • Players React. In combat, the characters and the bandits act on their turns.

Use the D&D Beyond Basic Rules to run this encounter.

Treasure

Stashed in the bushes are the recent ill-gotten gains stolen by Pral's band. If the characters defeat Pral and his band, they find a sack that contains 20 GP and one magic item; roll once on the Magic Items table in appendix A (rerolling duplicates) to determine the item.

Magic Items

Some treasure entries contain magic items, objects imbued with arcane might. Whenever a player character finds a magic item, roll on the Magic Items table in appendix A (rerolling duplicates) to determine the item.

The rules glossary in the D&D Beyond Basic Rules defines any capitalized rules such as Bright Light.

title: Module Inset
html:
Boxed Text

Text that appears in a box like the one in this section is meant to be read aloud or paraphrased when the characters first arrive at a location or under a specific circumstance, as described in the text.

Boxed text is included for the region in general and for each encounter in it. Read the region's boxed text aloud before choosing the encounter, then read the boxed text aloud for that encounter to begin it.

title: Module Inset

Random Tables

You can use tables like this one to randomly determine parts of the adventure. In this case, roll 1d4 to randomly determine what the characters encounter on the trail. Alternatively, you can forgo rolling and simply choose an encounter from the table.

title: Module Inset

Theater of the Mind

While the "Bandit Ambush" encounter later in this region uses a map, the "Looted Wagon" encounter happens in your collective imaginations!

title: Read-Aloud Note

title: Module Inset
html:
Ability Checks

When the outcome of an action is uncertain, the game uses a d20 roll to determine success or failure. This is called a D20 Test. An ability check is one type of D20 Test. Here's how to run the ability check in the "Looted Wagon" encounter:

  • Describe the Scene. Read the boxed text to paint a mental picture of the scene.
  • Ask the Players, "What Do You Do?" If the players aren't sure how to respond, suggest ways they could glean more information, like looking for tracks.
  • Narrate the Results. The Difficulty Class (DC) for each listed ability check is 13. This number represents the difficulty of the task. If the total of the d20 and its modifiers equals or exceeds 13, the check succeeds. On a 12 or lower, it fails. The encounter's description tells you what happens on a successful check. In this encounter, nothing happens on a failed check, but the character can try again.
  • Example. The Cleric searches the wagon and makes a Wisdom (Perception) check. The player rolls a d20 and adds their character's Perception modifier (+5) for a total of 17. The check succeeds, and the Cleric finds the treasure.

title: Module Inset
html:
Treasure

Treasure entries detail loot in an area, such as Gold Pieces (GP). Whenever a player character finds gold, give that player Gold Pieces equal to the listed value, which is tracked on their character sheet. Encourage players to split their treasure as evenly as possible.

title: Read-Aloud Note
html:
A young woman with a massive backpack and an eager smile hikes toward you along the trail. The traveler waves at you excitedly.

"Good day!" she says. "I'm Mallyn. Might you be adventurers? I ask because I've been out here looking for adventures of my own—to no avail. After camping out here for days, I still don't have any tales worth telling. Do you?"

title: Region 2: Woods
html:
Region 2: Woods

North of the keep sprawls a vast forest, home to hardy oaks, meaty mushrooms, and stores of primal magic. Wherever one goes in the woods, mystery and adventure abound.

Map: Woods

Woods Features

The woods have the following feature:

  • Lighting. The thick forest canopy filters sunlight from above, resulting in only Dim Light.

Getting Started

To begin, read the following boxed text aloud:

Dappled sunlight trickles through the canopy of this old-growth forest. Felled trees, shrubs, and mushrooms dot the forest floor.

Woods Encounters

Each time the characters explore this region, roll once on the Woods Encounters table to determine what the characters encounter.

Woods Encounters
1d4Encounter
1Hermit's Hut
2Occult Ritual
3Sacred Spring
4Sparring Sprites

Hermit's Hut

After a couple of hours of hiking, you happen on a humble hut made from sheets of sturdy bark and blankets of moss. Sweet-smelling smoke wafts from its chimney. The hut's wooden door is shut.

A hermit named Xanthe lives here. Banished months ago from the keep, Xanthe is initially Hostile [Attitude] toward the characters, who she believes have come to harass her.

A character who tries to convince Xanthe that they bear no ill will can make a 12 Charisma (Persuasion) check. A successful check improves Xanthe's attitude to Indifferent [Attitude], and the hermit invites the party into her hut, where she shares her story and the rumors on her NPC Card. On a failed check, Xanthe slams the door in their faces.

Xanthe

Elf Hermit

  • Statblock:. Commoner

One of the Borderlands' oldest and wisest residents was banished from the keep for crimes she didn't commit.

  • Bad Reputation. Xanthe was wrongfully exiled for using occult magic.
  • Distrustful. Xanthe doesn't trust strangers.
  • "A spy named Jacko prowls the fens. Be wary if you meet him. He'll do anything for coin—even kill." (True)
  • "The temple's head priest is a demon worshiper." (Partially true; Xanthe is referring to Ivlis, the former priest)

Occult Ritual

Eventually, you come across an eerie statue in a forest clearing. Strange runes are etched into the stone idol. Four human figures in occult robes gather around the statue, chanting ominously.

Four Cultist conduct a ritual around this ancient statue. They belong to the Cult of Chaos, a faction that delights in death and disarray. They are Hostile [Attitude] toward those not garbed in their cult's attire but don't immediately notice the characters.

The cultists continue intoning until their ritual is complete or interrupted. If disturbed, they fight.

Adjusting the Difficulty

To make this encounter easier, reduce the number of Cultist. Conversely, you can make this encounter more challenging by adding one or more Zombie, which aid the cultists as undead thralls.

Fooling the Cultists

The cultists are Indifferent [Attitude] toward any character wearing a Cultist's Robe, which they might have obtained in the Caves of Chaos (see "Caves of Chaos"). If a character approaches in this disguise, the cultists solemnly motion for the character to join the ritual, but they begin combat if the character refuses.

Completing the Ritual

If the characters join the ritual—or observe it without drawing attention—the statue's runes begin to glow with an eerie red light. After 10 minutes, the sky darkens, and the statue suddenly splits in two with a loud crack. Moments later, a wicked, disembodied laugh echoes throughout the forest. The cultists then disband.

Map: Woods (Occult Ritual)

Treasure

The characters can take robes from the defeated cultists. For each robe they take, give the players a Cultist's Robe.

Sacred Spring

Deep in the heart of the forest, the foliage parts to reveal a tranquil grove where a natural spring burbles. Rays of sunlight create a silvery glow about the crystal-clear pool.

This sacred spring is infused with primal magic.

Healing Water

A character who takes an action to drink from the spring regains 5 Hit Points. Once a character regains Hit Points from the spring, they can't do so again until they finish a Long Rest.

Destroying the Chaos Bell

If the party has the Chaos Bell from the Shrine of Evil Chaos (see "Caves of Chaos"), a character can submerge the evil artifact in this sacred spring. If this is done at night while the spring is bathed in moonlight, the bell turns to glittering ash.

Sparring Sprites

Farther into the woods, four diminutive, winged warriors flit between oversized toadstools and mossy logs, firing needlelike arrows from tiny bows. One of them calls out to you.

"Well met, giant travelers! We are training for battle," he reports. "Care to spar with us?"

Four Sprite Skirmisher spar vigorously in this clearing. The sprites are Indifferent [Attitude] toward the characters but interested in testing their mettle against the party.

Sparring with the Sprites

If the characters agree to spar with the pugnacious fey, the bout proceeds as a nonlethal combat encounter. The sprites bow gracefully, then ready their weapons. Roll Initiative.

The sprites fight valiantly but with restraint. A player character reduced to 0 Hit Points by a sprite has the Unconscious condition and is Stable. The sprites expect similar treatment by the characters.

If all the sprites are defeated, they quickly rouse themselves and commend the characters on their tactical prowess. If all the characters are defeated instead, the sprites wait for the characters to wake up—1 hour later and with 1 Hit Point each—to thank them for helping the sprites train.

Treasure

In exchange for the characters' spirited participation, the sprites reward the party with one magic item; roll once on the Magic Items table in appendix A (rerolling duplicates) to determine the item.

Map: Woods (Sparring Sprites)

title: Region 3: Fens
html:
Region 3: Fens

This sodden wetland is home to dangerous wildlife, canny foes, and squelching mud.

Map: Fens

Fens Features

The fens have the following features:

  • Lighting. The fens are in Bright Light.
  • Reeds. Tall, slender reeds grow throughout the soggy wetland. Areas with reeds are Lightly Obscured and Difficult Terrain.
  • Standing Water. Shallow, soupy pools of murk pervade the fens. The water is Difficult Terrain.

Getting Started

To begin, read the following boxed text aloud:

Mosquitoes buzz about the stands of cattails and gnarled trees in these squashy, stagnant fens. Croaking frogs, chirping cicadas, and squawking birds create an incessant din.

Fens Encounters

Each time the characters explore this region, roll once on the Fens Encounters table to determine what the characters encounter.

Fens Encounters
1d4Encounter
1Flock of Stirges
2Lizardfolk Swamp
3Spy's Campsite
4Sword Ferns

Flock of Stirges

Your journey halts at a narrow creek bed stained with blood. Near the shore, a giant river rat lies dead in the mud. The carcass is shriveled as if drained of its bodily fluids.

Suddenly, a flock of horrid creatures erupts from the reeds. Each has barbed, leathery wings and a long, sharp proboscis. Roll initiative!

Three Stirge descend on the characters. These bloodthirsty creatures can't be reasoned with; the Hostile [Attitude] stirges fight to the death.

Map: Fens (Flock of Stirges)

Adjusting the Difficulty

To make this encounter easier, you can reduce the number of Stirge, or you can increase the difficulty by adding one or more Gnoll Warrior drawn here by the scent of blood.

Lizardfolk Swamp

Deeper into the fens, mounds of mud rise above the fetid water and reeds. You spot a glint of gold amid the mud.

The fen's territorial lizardfolk denizens use these mounds to conceal their treasure. Two Lizardfolk Warden hide among the reeds, watching over the mounds. The lizardfolk have the Invisible condition and are Hostile [Attitude] toward the characters.

After 1 minute, the lizardfolk appear and tersely command the characters to leave at once. If the characters refuse, the lizardfolk fight.

Detecting the Lizardfolk

As a Search action, a character can scan the mud mounds for signs of danger, detecting the lizardfolk with a successful 15 Wisdom (Perception) check.

Fighting the Lizardfolk

If a character approaches the mound or disturbs the treasure (see below), the lizardfolk leap out and start combat. Characters who failed to detect the lizardfolk before the ambush have Disadvantage on their Initiative rolls. The lizardfolk fight fiercely in defense of their possessions.

Treasure

Hidden in the mounds are 20 GP and one gemstone (worth 100 GP).

Map: Fens (Lizardfolk Swamp)

Spy's Campsite

The air is still in this corner of the fens. Just ahead, a curved stand of reeds conceals a secluded campsite with a still-smoldering firepit. The reeds sway and rustle in the muggy breeze.

This campsite belongs to Jacko, a notorious spy for hire. Jacko hides in the surrounding foliage. He is Indifferent [Attitude] toward the characters.

Detecting Jacko

As a Search action, a character can survey the campsite for clues to its inhabitant's whereabouts and make one of the following ability checks. Consider these examples:

15 Wisdom (Perception). The character spots the glint of Jacko's blade in the reeds.

15 Wisdom (Survival). The character spots faint tracks that lead to the spy.

On a successful check, Jacko emerges from the tall reeds and commends the party on finding his hideout. He then offers his services to the party.

Hiring Jacko

Plucky do-gooders aren't Jacko's usual clientele, but for 25 GP, he offers to join the characters in a single fight anywhere in the wilderness. If the party contains a Rogue or a character with the Criminal background, Jacko offers a 5 GP discount. The shady halfling advertises his services as "all inclusive" and "no questions asked" while performing a cutthroat gesture.

If a player character hires Jacko, whenever the characters roll Initiative in the wilderness, ask that player if they'd like Jacko to assist them in the fight. If so, Jacko joins the fray alongside the party. After the fight, Jacko returns to this location unless the characters hire him again.

Sword Ferns

As you trudge through the mud, you tumble into a ravine of razor-sharp ferns. To continue, you must navigate this treacherous gully.

A character who examines the ferns can make a 12 Intelligence (Nature) check, identifying the plants as sword ferns—bladelike ferns endemic to jungles and wetlands—on a successful check.

To forge a path through the ferns, each character must succeed on one of the following checks:

15 Strength (Athletics). The character hacks a path through the ferns with a weapon or stick.

15 Wisdom (Survival). The character finds a safe trail through the ferns used by wild animals.

On a failed check, the character takes 1d6 Slashing damage from the ferns on their way through the gully.

title: Region 4: Tamarack Stand
html:
Region 4: Tamarack Stand

This hilly region's sparse trees have short, bristly needles. Forest fires and giant animals are more common in this stretch of the wilds.

Map: Tamarack Stand

Tamarack Stand Features

The tamarack stand has the following feature:

  • Lighting. Bright Light illuminates the region.

Getting Started

To begin, read the following boxed text aloud:

Conifers rise from this highland's soft, peaty soil. Squirrels skitter about the fallen pinecones and pine needles that blanket the ground.

Tamarack Stand Encounters

Each time the characters explore this region, roll once on the Tamarack Stand Encounters table to determine what the characters encounter.

Tamarack Stand Encounters
1d4Encounter
1Flash Fire
2Giant Spiders' Nest
3Hobgoblin Patrol
4Pine Seeds

Flash Fire

Your expedition stops at the bottom of a steep gorge—a dead end. As you reorient yourselves, smoke begins to fill the air, and a sudden forest fire spreads through the dry canyon.

The conflagration roars in the party's direction, engulfing everything in its path.

To escape the fire unscathed, each character must succeed on one of the following ability checks:

15 Strength (Athletics). The character scales the gorge to safety.

15 Dexterity (Acrobatics). The character leaps across the branches, avoiding the flames below.

15 Wisdom (Survival). The character cuts through a thicket of trees with fire-resistant sap.

On a failed check, a character takes 2d6 Fire damage on their way to safety.

Giant Spiders' Nest

You wander into a maze of thick webs camouflaged between tall trees. Two massive arachnids descend on you with fangs bared.

Two Giant Spider start combat, eager to make the characters their next meal.

Some characters begin this encounter trapped in the spiders' sticky web (see the "Giant Web" section). Roll a die for each character. On an odd number, the character starts their turn in the web.

Giant Webs

The giant spiders have woven a 20-foot Cube [Area of Effect] of thick, sticky webs between the trees to snare prey. The webs are Difficult Terrain, and the area within them is Lightly Obscured.

The first time a creature enters the webs on a turn or starts its turn there, it must succeed on a 12 Dexterity saving throw or have the Restrained condition until it breaks free or the webs are destroyed.

As an action, a creature Restrained by the webs can make a 12 Strength (Athletics) check. If it succeeds, it is no longer Restrained.

The webs are flammable and laden with dry pollen and old animal carcasses. If the webs take Fire damage, the entire 20-foot Cube of webs ignites, and each creature Restrained by the webs takes 2d4 Fire damage. The webs then burn away and are destroyed at the end of the turn.

Treasure

After the fight, the characters find one magic item suspended in the webs; roll once on the Magic Items table in appendix A (rerolling duplicates) to determine the item.

Map: Tamarack Stand (Giant Spiders' Nest)

Hobgoblin Patrol

Ahead of you, three humanoid warriors in battered armor argue in harsh tones as they march through the forest. They haven't noticed you yet.

Three Hobgoblin Warrior were recently separated from their squadron after a bitter defeat. The Hostile [Attitude] hobgoblins are ornery and assault the characters on sight.

Adjusting the Difficulty

To make this encounter easier, you can reduce the number of Hobgoblin Warrior. Conversely, add one more Hobgoblin Warrior to increase the difficulty.

Eavesdropping on the Hobgoblins

To listen in on the hobgoblins' argument, a character must come within 30 feet of the patrol and make a 15 Dexterity (Stealth) check. On a successful check, the character hears the hobgoblins debating whether they should ally with the bugbears in the Caves of Chaos or hire the ogre mercenary that dwells there (both are detailed in "Caves of Chaos"). On a failed check, the hobgoblins spot the eavesdropping character and start combat.

Treasure

Each hobgoblin carries a leather pouch that contains 4 GP.

Map: Tamarack Stand (Hobgoblin Patrol)

Pine Seeds

Two types of trees grow in this area: one with russet bark and ruby-red pinecones, and another with gray bark and green pinecones. Squirrels and voles scamper about, collecting seeds from fallen cones. After so much travel, your stomachs growl with hunger.

The pine seeds from either tree are tasty, but the seeds from the ruby-red pinecones are poisonous.

A character can try to identify the edible pine seeds and make one of the following ability checks. Consider these examples:

13 Intelligence (Nature). The character identifies both trees and which seeds are edible.

13 Wisdom (Survival). The character observes that local woodland critters eat pine seeds only from the green pinecones.

On a failed check, a character accidentally gathers the poisonous seeds.

Poisonous Pine Seeds

A creature that eats the seeds of a ruby-red pinecone must succeed on a 15 Constitution saving throw or have the Poisoned condition until it finishes a Long Rest.
